figures.title: Contiguous reservation wastes the tail; paged blocks waste only the last block
figures.caption: Orca-style contiguous allocation holds the worst-case share for a sequence's whole life, so a 100-token reply reserves 65,536 positions and leaves 65,436 idle. PagedAttention allocates 16-position blocks on demand: the same request takes seven blocks, 112 positions, with 12 positions of tail waste.
figures.alt: Two aligned panels. The contiguous panel reserves 65,536 positions per stream from admission, so a 100-token reply leaves 65,436 positions idle for its whole life; the note records that only 20 to 40 percent of reserved KV memory held token state in the vLLM measurements. The paged panel allocates 16-position physical blocks: 100 tokens need seven blocks, 112 positions, and only the last block's 12 positions are wasted.

anim.intro: Press Play or Next to compare a worst-case reservation with 16-position blocks.

steps.label: A reserving engine gives each of four streams an equal 262,144 / 4 = 65,536 positions, held from admission for the request's whole life.
A 100-token reply still holds its full 65,536-position share, so 65,536 − 100 = 65,436 positions sit idle.
Paging allocates 16-position physical blocks on demand instead.
100 tokens take 100 / 16 = 6.25, so 7 blocks: six full and one holding 4 tokens.
7 x 16 = 112 positions against 100 tokens leaves 112 − 100 = 12 positions of tail waste, and the waste cannot exceed one block.

figures.title: A block table is the indirection that makes sharing and copy-on-write cheap
figures.caption: A 100-token prompt fills seven 16-position blocks whose physical ids are 7, 12, 3, 19, 22, 8, and 41. After B forks, both block tables point at the same blocks with refcount 2; when B writes into logical block 6, the engine copies physical block 41 into free block 55 and drops 41 to refcount 1.
figures.alt: A memory strip showing eight occupied physical block ids scattered across a 64-block window: 7, 12, 3, 19, 22, 8, 41 for request A, and 55 as B's copy. Below it a table maps logical blocks 0 through 6 to those physical blocks with refcount 2, plus logical block 6 for B mapped to physical block 55 with refcount 1.

table.title: A's block table: logical to physical to refcount

data.note: The strip is a 64-block window of a pool that holds 262,144 positions, 16 per block. Scattered physical blocks are free placement; the table is what turns them back into a contiguous logical sequence.

anim.intro: Press Play or Next to fork a sequence and watch the reference count force one copy.

steps.label: A's 100-token prompt occupies seven 16-position blocks: logical blocks 0 to 6 map to physical 7, 12, 3, 19, 22, 8, and 41, scattered anywhere in the pool.
Fork into A and B: both block tables point at those same seven physical blocks, so every refcount rises from 1 to 2 and nothing is copied.
B generates token 101 in logical block 6. Its refcount is 2, so the engine takes a free block, 55, copies block 41 into it, rewrites B's entry 6, and decrements 41 to 1; A's table is untouched.

figures.title: Block size trades tail waste against table entries
figures.caption: On the same 100-token sequence, smaller blocks cut waste and multiply table entries: 8-position blocks waste 4 positions and need 13 entries, 16-position blocks waste 12 and need 7, and 64-position blocks waste 28 and need 2. The kernel walks every entry to gather a sequence's blocks, so 16 is the common default.
figures.alt: Four horizontal bars of tail waste for a 100-token sequence. Block size 8 wastes 4 positions and needs 13 table entries. Block size 16 wastes 12 positions and needs 7 entries. Block size 32 wastes 28 positions and needs 4 entries. Block size 64 wastes 28 positions and needs 2 entries.

data.note: Tail waste is the unused tail of the last block; entries are the block-table rows the gather walks. Sixteen positions is the common default.

anim.intro: Press Play or Next to trade tail waste against table entries for a 100-token sequence.

steps.label: Block size 8: 100 / 8 = 12.5, so 13 blocks; twelve are full and the last holds 4 tokens, leaving 4 positions of tail waste and 13 entries to chase.
Block size 16: 100 / 16 = 6.25, so 7 blocks; 7 x 16 = 112, leaving 12 of tail waste and 7 entries.
Block size 32: 100 / 32 = 3.125, so 4 blocks; 4 x 32 = 128, leaving 28 of tail waste and 4 entries.
Block size 64: 100 / 64 = 1.5625, so 2 blocks covering 128 positions, the same 28 of tail waste with only 2 entries.

sources.note: Kwon et al., PagedAttention: the 20-40 percent reservation figure, block tables, copy-on-write sharing, and the 2-4x throughput result.
Yu et al., Orca: the contiguous worst-case reservation this chapter replaces.
